newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - It's Erubis forever among Japan faithful.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - It's Erubis forever among Japan faithful.

text.p: It's a steamy summer weekend in the Ginza, Tokyo's glitziest entertainment and shopping district, and "Erubisu Puresuri" has just left the building, sequins and slick bouffant sparkling in the neon night.

Three Erubisu Puresuris, to be precise: Japanese Elvis Presley impersonators, who -- costumes and coiffure aside -- don't look much like the King of Rock and Roll. They don't even speak English, they admit.

But on stage in a Ginza nightclub devoted to 1950s American rock and roll, these Elvises sweat sincerity and sing with an authority that belies the fact they were barely out of grade school when Presley died on August 16, 1977.

A crowd gathered for a party to mark the 20th anniversary of Presley's death are thirtyish, Budweiser-sipping Japanese, most of the men with hair slicked back and some wearing 1950s style bowling shirts embroidered with names like "Tony De Rosa's Garage". A few women wear hoop skirts.
TO MEMPHIS WITH LOVE

The party was a week earlier than the actual anniversary on Saturday because some Japanese Elvises and many in the audience -- made up mostly of members of the Elvis Presley Fan Club (Tokyo Branch) -- will be in Memphis, Tennessee that day.
"I'll be making the pilgrimage to Memphis," said Naoto Ogata, 31, a tall and handsome full-time singer who calls himself the "Sapporo Elvis" after his northern Japan hometown.

"I had no idea who or what Elvis was when he died -- I was in sixth grade. But when I began my music career, his greatness dawned on me," said Ogata, still dripping wet from a ripping rendition of "Blue Suede Shoes".

Tomokazu Taguchi, 36, owner of the club and an Elvis impersonator himself has been to Presley's grave and Graceland Mansion in Memphis five times, he said, but will be performing on the 16th, as he does every year to mark that day.
"Elvis is an immense presence in my life," said Taguchi, beaming reverently in a white imitation leather jumpsuit studded with hundreds of rhinestones.
"Hearing his songs, I came to appreciate the joy of music of all kinds and even the joy of living," he said.

On the actual death anniversary -- which, appropriately enough, follows the three-day Obon festival in which Japanese Buddhists welcome their ancestors' souls, the Tokyo Elvis' fan club will host a seven-hour "Elvis Forever" festival featuring impersonators and films.
The satellite channel run by NHK public television is marking the event by showing Presley's major movies.
UNLIKELY ICON
Many first-time U.S. visitors to Japan are astonished to find a country they'd believed to be impregnable to U.S. imports awash with American cinema, pop and sports stars.
But why has Elvis' fan club in Japan grown from 300 members at the time of his death to about 10,000 now?
Unlike American icons such as Harrison Ford, Madonna and Dennis Rodman -- who visit Tokyo on occasion and are widely recognised from television -- Elvis had his heyday before Japan's TV age.

And unlike the Rolling Stones, he never performed in Tokyo, much less sold out the Tokyo Dome. And his death, of a junk food- and drug-induced heart attack at 42, was not the stuff of legends, even fans admit.

"To be honest, Elvis has never had a great reputation here," said Billy Morokawa, author of two books about Presley and a rockabilly guitarist and singer who has recorded in Memphis with former members of the king's band.
"Ask Japanese what they know about Elvis," said Morokawa. "They'll tell you he died from a donut overdose, was fat and wore gaudy outfits -- in a word, tacky!

"But he was a great musician and that's what I want people to know. I'm confident that his music will appeal to anyone who hears it, transcending language and race from China to Spain," says Morokawa.
ROLE MODEL, LIBERATOR
Many of the Elvis faithful in Japan are musicians who fell in love with the man through his music, said Morokawa, who is in his late thirties and bought Presley's records as a teenager.
"He was the image of the ideal man I wanted to become -- the way I thought a man should live his life," he told Reuters between sets of very credible versions of early Elvis hits.
"His music gives me a feeling of liberation, the sense that I can do anything," he said.
But Elvis worship is not only a "guy thing", insists Saori Koga, an actress in a rockabilly musical opening later in August.
"He was slim and handsome when he was young, but I honestly think his appeal as a male increased with age -- even though he got chunky," said the 29-year-old stage performer.
Asked about the alleged Elvis sightings in the United States, the Japanese Erubisus smile at the notion the king is still among the living.
"I'm sure that Elvis' spirit lives on in our hearts, but his body is most assuredly dead," said Morokawa.
